## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Create vectors with `c()`, `:`, `seq()` and `rep()`.
2. Calculate with a whole vector at once.
3. Summarise a vector with `sum()`, `mean()`, `max()` and similar functions, including when values are missing.
4. Pick out values by position, by name and by a condition.
5. Explain why every value in a vector has the same type.

## What is a vector?

A **vector** is a sequence of values of the same type. It is the most important structure in R. Even a single number is a vector of length 1, which is why R prints `[1]` in front of it.

Create a vector with `c()`, which stands for "combine":

```{webr}
household_size <- c(4, 6, 2, 7, 5, 3)
household_size
length(household_size)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
A vector is like a single column in a spreadsheet. Tomorrow you will put several vectors side by side to make a table.
:::

### Other ways to make vectors

```{webr}
1:10                          # whole numbers from 1 to 10
seq(0, 100, by = 25)          # from 0 to 100 in steps of 25
rep("Yes", times = 3)         # repeat a value
c("Gulu", "Arua", "Mbale")    # character vector
```

## Calculating with vectors

Arithmetic on a vector applies to every value. This is called **vectorisation**, and it is why R code is often short.

```{webr}
prices_ugx <- c(2500, 800, 12000, 4500)
prices_ugx * 1.18             # add 18% VAT to every price
prices_ugx / 3800             # convert every price to US dollars
```

Two vectors of the same length are combined value by value:

```{webr}
quantity <- c(3, 2, 1, 4)
prices_ugx * quantity         # cost of each line
```

## Summary functions

These functions take a whole vector and return one value:

```{webr}
sum(household_size)
mean(household_size)
median(household_size)
min(household_size)
max(household_size)
sd(household_size)            # standard deviation
```

### When values are missing

If any value is `NA`, the summary is `NA` too. Add `na.rm = TRUE` to leave missing values out:

```{webr}
ages <- c(34, NA, 27, 41, NA, 19)
mean(ages)
mean(ages, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(ages))              # how many values are missing?
```

`sum(is.na(ages))` works because `is.na()` gives `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each value, and R counts `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE` as 0.

## Picking out values (indexing)

Use square brackets `[ ]` to pick values from a vector.

### By position

```{webr}
towns <- c("Gulu", "Arua", "Mbale", "Jinja", "Lira")
towns[1]          # the first value. R counts from 1, not 0.
towns[c(2, 4)]    # the second and fourth values
towns[2:4]        # the second to the fourth
towns[-1]         # everything except the first
```

### By name

You can give each value a name, then pick values by name:

```{webr}
population <- c(Gulu = 150000, Arua = 72000, Mbale = 97000)
population["Arua"]
names(population)
```

### By a condition

This is the most useful kind of indexing. Write a comparison inside the brackets, and R keeps the values where the answer is `TRUE`:

```{webr}
household_size > 4                    # TRUE/FALSE for each value
household_size[household_size > 4]    # keep only those values
```

Combine conditions with `&` (and) and `|` (or):

```{webr}
household_size[household_size >= 3 & household_size <= 5]
towns[towns == "Gulu" | towns == "Lira"]
towns[towns %in% c("Gulu", "Lira")]   # shorter way to write the line above
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
Indexing by a condition does the same job as a filter on an Excel column.
:::

## One type per vector

A vector can hold only one type. If you mix types, R converts everything to the most flexible one, usually character:

```{webr}
mixed <- c(1, "two", 3)
mixed
class(mixed)
```

The numbers have become text. This is called **coercion**. It often explains surprising results when you import data: a single text value in a column of numbers turns the whole column into text.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Create a vector

Create a vector called `rainfall` with these monthly rainfall values in millimetres: 120, 85, 60, 140, 175. Then calculate the total.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_create
rainfall <- ______
sum(rainfall)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex3_create"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Use `c()` and put commas between the values.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex3_create"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
rainfall <- c(120, 85, 60, 140, 175)
sum(rainfall)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_create
#| check: true
if (!exists("rainfall") || length(rainfall) != 5) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "rainfall should contain 5 values.")
} else if (!isTRUE(all.equal(rainfall, c(120, 85, 60, 140, 175)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Check the values in rainfall.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 580))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 580 mm in total.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "rainfall is right. The last line should give its sum.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Vectorised maths

Temperatures are recorded in Celsius. Convert all of them to Fahrenheit using the formula *F = C × 9 / 5 + 32*.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_temp
#| setup: true
celsius <- c(18, 22, 25, 29, 31)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_temp
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex3_temp"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
You do not need a loop. Write the formula once, using `celsius` in place of *C*.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex3_temp"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_temp
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, celsius * 9 / 5 + 32))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. One line converts every value.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You should get 5 values, starting with 64.4.")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Mean with missing values

Some test scores are missing. Calculate the average of the scores you have.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_mean
#| setup: true
scores <- c(72, 85, NA, 64, 90, NA, 78)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_mean
mean(scores, ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex3_mean"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Add the argument that removes `NA` values before calculating.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex3_mean"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_mean
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 77.8))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 77.8.")
} else if (identical(.result, NA_real_)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You got NA. Add na.rm = TRUE.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. The answer is 77.8.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Index by position

Get the **last three** towns from the vector `towns`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_position
#| setup: true
towns <- c("Gulu", "Arua", "Mbale", "Jinja", "Lira", "Hoima")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_position
towns[______]
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex3_position"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
There are 6 towns. The last three are at positions 4, 5 and 6. Use `:` to write a range.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex3_position"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
towns[4:6]
```
A version that works for any length is `towns[(length(towns) - 2):length(towns)]`.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_position
#| check: true
if (identical(.result, c("Jinja", "Lira", "Hoima"))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You should get Jinja, Lira and Hoima, in that order.")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Filter with a condition

Keep only the households with **more than 5** members.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_filter
#| setup: true
household_size <- c(4, 6, 2, 7, 5, 3, 9, 1)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_filter
household_size[______]
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex3_filter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Put a comparison inside the brackets: `household_size > ______`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex3_filter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
household_size[household_size > 5]
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3_filter
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, c(6, 7, 9)))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 6, 7 and 9.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, c(6, 7, 5, 9)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You included 5. 'More than 5' means > 5, not >= 5.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You should get 6, 7 and 9.")
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting `c()`.** `mean(1, 2, 3)` gives 1, because `mean()` only reads the first argument as the data. Write `mean(c(1, 2, 3))`.
- **Counting from 0.** The first value is `x[1]`. `x[0]` gives an empty vector.
- **Forgetting `na.rm = TRUE`.** A single `NA` makes `sum()` and `mean()` return `NA`.
- **Writing `x > 3 & < 8`.** Repeat the object: `x > 3 & x < 8`.
- **Mixing types by accident.** One text value turns a whole vector into text. Check with `class()`.

## Summary

- A vector holds many values of one type. Create one with `c()`, `:`, `seq()` or `rep()`.
- Maths on a vector applies to every value at once.
- `sum()`, `mean()`, `median()`, `min()`, `max()` and `sd()` summarise a vector. Use `na.rm = TRUE` to skip missing values.
- Pick values with `[ ]`: by position (`x[2]`), by name (`x["Gulu"]`) or by a condition (`x[x > 5]`).
- Combine conditions with `&` and `|`. Use `%in%` to match against a list of values.

**Tomorrow:** you will put vectors side by side to make data frames, the R version of a spreadsheet table.
